prompt: What exactly causes volcanoes to form?
first_answer: Volcanoes form due to the Earth's internal heat. The Earth's crust is made up of tectonic plates that float on a semi-fluid layer in the mantle. Where these plates meet, one can either move past the other (this is called a divergent boundary) or one can move under the other (this is called a convergent boundary). At divergent boundaries, magma rises to the surface, creating a volcanic mountain range. At convergent boundaries, especially where one plate made of oceanic crust (which is denser) moves under another plate made of continental crust (which is less dense), the intense heat and pressure cause the oceanic plate to melt. This melted rock, or magma, then rises towards the surface and can erupt through weak spots in the overlying plate to form volcanoes on the continental crust. Volcanoes can also form over hotspots, which are plumes of hot material that rise from the Earth's mantle and cause melting at the base of the lithosphere (the rigid outer layer of the Earth). These hotspots are thought to be relatively stationary as the tectonic plates move over them, leading to chains of volcanoes.
